Amortized Deliberation: Practice and the Dual-Process

                          Partition


                                    Flyxion
                          Independent Researcher

                               October 2026



                                           Abstract

     The dual-process vocabulary of a fast, automatic “System 1” and a slow, deliberate “Sys-
     tem 2” is routinely applied to individual thoughts, tasks and, more recently, to classes of
     machine models. The observable basis for the division is speed, effort and reportability.
      This essay argues that these cannot by themselves identify two kinds of thought, because
      each is a property of a task together with a history of practice and not of the task alone.
    A reversal argument, with the keypad as its standard example, shows that no history-
     independent set of tasks separates easy from hard across a pair whose cost order reverses
     with practice. A one-process model in which practice amortizes earlier evaluation, with
       retrieval, applicability and fallback costs stated explicitly, reproduces the continuous prac-
       tice curve and the apparent fast and slow regimes. A routing argument shows that a cat-
      egorical sorter does no further explanatory work in that model, though it is not excluded.
     The shape of a cost distribution, including bimodality, is shown to underdetermine the
     number of mechanisms. Two illustrations are used. The ﬁrst is a cached decision archi-
       tecture, whose cost is an explicit continuous function of how much computation has been
     precomputed while its outputs are unchanged. The second is a progress-aligned recurrent
     model, in which practice supports reusable sequential computation that extends beyond
      the training length without externalized text. Together they indicate that learning history,
      representation, execution and reuse explain variation in cost, and that a division into two
      systems is neither needed for that explanation nor identiﬁed by the evidence. What sur-
      vives of the distinction is a set of distinguishable dimensions.


1  The Content of a Partition Claim


The inference from differences in speed to differences in cognitive kind requires additional
assumptions, and the dual-process vocabulary is used with at least three different commit-
ments. On one interpretation, tasks themselves belong to history-independent classes, so that
a thought is fast or slow whoever thinks it. On a second, the classes are mechanisms whose


                                        1

engagement depends on the agent and the situation, and a given thought is handled by one
or the other according to circumstance. On a third, the vocabulary is merely descriptive of
speed and effort and speciﬁes no architecture. These interpretations must be distinguished,
because evidence against an intrinsic partition of tasks does not by itself establish that only
one mechanism operates. The popular form of the doctrine adds a further element, which
is that the slow mechanism is the one associated with awareness, effort and the self, and the
fast mechanism is what remains once those are subtracted, and a dispatcher that assigns each
thought to its mechanism is often posited. The vocabulary was given its widest currency by
Kahneman (2011), and the original two-systems reading has been criticized as a conﬂation of
several independent dimensions (Keren and Schul 2009; Melnikoff and Bargh 2018).
   The most careful current statement of the dual-process view is that of Evans and Stanovich
(2013), who separate the deﬁning characteristics of the two types of processing from the at-
tributes that merely tend to accompany them. On their account Type 1 processing is deﬁned
by autonomy, meaning that it does not require working memory or controlled attention, and
Type 2 processing is deﬁned by its dependence on working memory and by cognitive de-
coupling, the capacity for hypothetical thinking. Speed, effort, high capacity and association
with consciousness are treated as correlates and not as deﬁnitions. The target of this essay
is narrower than the whole of that position. The reversal argument below bears directly on
classiﬁcations inferred from cost, since a ranking by speed or effort is a ranking by correlated
attributes and the argument shows that such rankings depend on history.  It leaves the pro-
posed deﬁning characteristics, autonomy and the use of working memory for decoupling,
as questions for further investigation. Two cautions apply to them. A response that begins
as a decoupled, working-memory-dependent computation can become autonomous through
practice, so autonomy is itself history-dependent. And the deﬁning characteristics are prop-
erties of processes. Attributing these characteristics to tasks independently of history would
require a further argument; the reversal result concerns cost separation rather than autonomy
or working-memory dependence directly.
   The difﬁculty with inferring a partition from behaviour is that the behaviour in question,
which is speed, depends on history. A thought is a computation performed by a particular
agent at a particular time, and its cost depends on what that agent has already computed. The
same sum is hard for a child and effortless for an adult, and this is not a fact about the sum.
The partition claim treats the endpoints of a practice curve as if they were the outputs of two
different machines. The present essay formalizes a single-process alternative in which cost
falls with accumulated experience, and shows that the observations usually cited in favour of
the partition are what such a process predicts, so that they cannot by themselves discriminate
between the accounts. The claim defended is deliberately of two strengths. The formal results
establish that a partition of tasks or of mechanisms cannot be inferred from speed alone. The
further position, that no partition of mechanisms is needed, is argued from parsimony and


                                         2

from worked models, and it is not offered as a theorem.


2  Setting

Let T be a set of tasks and H a set of histories, where a history h ∈H records everything
an agent has previously done that bears on its performance. Let C  : T × H →R>0 assign
to each task and history the resource cost of producing an adequate response, measured in
whatever units are convenient, such as time, error-corrected attempts or arithmetic operations.
A history is a partial record of past episodes, and for a task t we write nh(t) for the number of
prior episodes in h that are relevant to t.

Deﬁnition 1 (History-independent cost separation). A set E ⊆T  is cost-separating at h if
C(t, h) < C(t′, h) for all t ∈E and t′ /∈E. It is intrinsic if it is cost-separating at every h ∈H.

  A partition of tasks into fast and slow that is read off from observed speed would need to
be a set of this kind, since otherwise the grouping changes when the agent’s history changes.
A theory might instead classify processes, or classify tasks relative to an agent and a history,
and the proposition below does not touch such theories directly.  Its target is the inference
from observed speed to a partition of tasks.


3  Difﬁculty Is a Relation

Deﬁnition 2 (Reversal pair). Tasks t, t′ form a reversal pair if there are histories h, h′ with
C(t, h) < C(t′, h) and C(t, h′) > C(t′, h′).

Proposition 1 (No intrinsic partition across a reversal).  If E contains exactly one member of a
reversal pair, then E is not intrinsic.

Proof. Say t ∈E and t′ /∈E. At h′ we have C(t, h′) > C(t′, h′), which violates the requirement
that every member of E be cheaper than every non-member. Hence E is not cost-separating
at h′. The argument is symmetric if t′ ∈E and t /∈E and one uses h.

   The proposition does not say that every set is non-intrinsic. A set containing both mem-
bers of every reversal pair, or neither, escapes it, and a population whose histories are drawn
from a common practice distribution may contain a set that is cost-separating for every his-
tory in that population. Such a set would be a fact about the population’s training, and it
could fail when the distribution of histories changed. Nor does the proposition rule out two
mechanisms whose relative engagement changes with practice. What it establishes is nar-
rower: a partition of tasks inferred from speed cannot establish a partition of mechanisms,
because speed depends on history. Showing that there is only one mechanism requires fur-
ther evidence, and the sections below supply an argument and models, not a proof.


                                         3

Example 1 (The keypad). A telephone arranges its digits with 1 2 3 in the top row, and a
calculator arranges them with 7 8 9 in the top row. Let t be entering a ﬁxed four-digit number
on the telephone layout and t′ be entering the same number on the calculator layout. Let h be
the history of someone who has used telephones for years and calculators rarely, and h′ the
converse. Under these stipulated histories, which are plausible and not measured, C(t, h) <
C(t′, h) and C(t, h′) > C(t′, h′). The task is identical in every respect that bears on its content,
namely the same digits in the same order, and the ordering of cost ﬂips with the history. Any
set E that contains one of the two entries and not the other is therefore history-dependent by
Proposition 1.

   The same structure appears with a door that pushes or pulls, an appliance whose controls
are laid out differently from the one previously used, or a language whose word order dif-
fers from the speaker’s own. In each case the cost of the task is a joint property of the task
and the practice behind it. The reversal argument applies wherever practice is task-speciﬁc.
Where two tasks differ mainly in how much they have been rehearsed, and not in irreducible
demands or attainable performance, their cost order can be exchanged by exchanging the
rehearsal, and not every pair of tasks is of this kind.


4  Practice as Amortization


The standard empirical regularity is the power law of practice (Newell and Rosenbloom 1981),
according to which cost after n relevant episodes is well described by

                        c(n) = a + b n−β,     a ≥0, b > 0, β > 0.                          (1)


Other forms, such as exponentials, ﬁt some data better, and Heathcote, Brown and Mewhort
(2000) argue that a power law in averaged curves can arise from averaging over participants
and items whose individual curves are exponential, so that the aggregate form does not iden-
tify the form of individual learning. The curve is therefore a stipulated illustration and not a
universal empirical law, and nothing below depends on the particular form. What matters is
that c is continuous, strictly decreasing and without a distinguished point.

Proposition 2 (No privileged threshold). For any threshold θ >  a, the number of episodes at
                                                 (which the stipulated cost ﬁrst falls to θ is n∗(θ) =  b/(θ −a) )1/β.  The map θ 7→n∗(θ) is a
continuous bijection from (a, ∞) onto (0, ∞), and the derivative c′(n) = −bβn−β−1 is continuous
and nonvanishing on (0, ∞).

Proof. Solve a + b n−β = θ for n. The remaining claims are direct computations.

  No value of θ corresponds to a distinguished point of the curve, since c′ is continuous
and nonvanishing, and the choice of θ belongs to the observer and not to c. Any statement


                                         4

of the form “the task became automatic after n∗repetitions” is therefore a statement about
the threshold θ chosen by the observer, since different choices move n∗over the entire pos-
itive half-line, and the stipulated curve itself contains no step. This bears on a particular
family of hypotheses, namely those that posit a discontinuous and behaviourally observable
switch from one mechanism to another, which would predict a gap in the cost or practice
axis. It does not bear on all two-mechanism accounts. Two mechanisms whose probabilities
of engagement change gradually, or which operate concurrently with changing relative con-
tributions, also produce continuous performance curves, and a single mechanism can show
abrupt transitions. Continuity therefore does not exclude two mechanisms. What it shows is
that crossing a threshold is not evidence of a switch.
   The mechanism behind the curve can be made explicit with a memoization model, in
the spirit of the instance theory of automatization (Logan 1988), in which automaticity is the
retrieval of stored episodes. Anderson (1982) supplies a complementary account, in which
knowledge compilation, through proceduralization and composition, converts knowledge
that is executed interpretively into productions that run directly, so that practice can change
a response by compiling a procedure and not only by storing an instance. Neither account,
taken alone, establishes that cognition uses one mechanism. The model has to be executable
and not merely an envelope of attainable costs, because an agent cannot take the cheaper
of two routes without ﬁrst paying to ﬁnd out which is cheaper. Let M be a store of solved
instances. Let S(t) be the cost of solving t from scratch, including the checking of the re-
sult. Retrieving the nearest stored case costs ℓ, and assessing whether that case applies to the
present task costs α. If it applies, which happens with probability π(t, M), the case is adapted
at expected cost ¯δ(t, M), where adaptation cost is a nondecreasing function δ(d) of the dis-
tance d between the task and the stored case, with δ(0) = 0, and δ is assumed continuous. If
it does not apply, the agent falls back on solving from scratch after having paid for retrieval
and assessment. The expected cost is

                                                      (           )
                 C(t | M) = ℓ+ α + π(t, M) ¯δ(t, M) + 1 −π(t, M)  S(t).                  (2)


Equation (2) explicitly includes the overhead of unsuccessful reuse attempts, namely retrieval
and assessment that end in fallback, and so it is not the minimum of the costs of the two routes.

Proposition 3 (Gradual improvement under growing coverage). Fix ℓ, α, ¯δ and S > ℓ+ α + ¯δ,
so that the stored route is cheaper than solving afresh, and let πn be the probability that the nearest
stored case applies at the nth encounter, with πn nondecreasing in n and πn →1. Then the expected
cost at the nth encounter is nonincreasing in n and converges to ℓ+ α + ¯δ, which is the cost when a
stored case always applies. The limit is forced by πn →1, and the improvement is gradual exactly to
the extent that πn is, so that if πn is continuous and strictly increasing in a continuous measure of
experience, the expected cost is continuous and strictly decreasing in it.


                                        5

Proof. From Equation (2), the expected cost is ℓ+ α + ¯δ + (1 −πn)(S −¯δ), which decreases as
πn increases, and S > ¯δ follows from the stated inequality. The limit follows from πn →1.

Remark 1. In the special case where the ﬁrst encounter pays S and every later encounter
retrieves the stored result at cost ℓ, the cumulative mean cost per episode is ℓ+ (S −ℓ)/n. This
decreases smoothly even though the per-episode costs are S, ℓ, ℓ, . . ., so it describes average
expenditure and not the current performance of the agent. Gradual improvement in current
performance requires an assumption of the kind in Proposition 3, such as growing coverage,
falling retrieval latency or rising applicability.

    Item-level evidence bears on the coverage assumption. Rickard (2004) reports item-level
tests of candidate models of the transition from algorithmic computation to memory retrieval
in skill learning, and such tests treat learning history as acting on particular items and not on
a task category as a whole. That supports treating the applicability probability as a property
of items and cases, and it supports history-sensitive change in which strategy is used.  It
concerns which strategy is used on which item, and it does not by itself settle whether the
strategies are separate architectural mechanisms.
   Equation (2) describes one process with one store and two ways of producing an answer,
in which the route taken is determined by how close the nearest stored case is and whether
it applies. Where applicability remains reliable and adaptation cost varies continuously with
distance, small differences from a stored case can incur small additional costs. Continuity
of adaptation cost does not by itself ensure continuity of the applicability probability, and
an assessment that fails can trigger an expensive fallback, so the cost of a task near a stored
case can change abruptly where applicability does. A task far from every stored case costs
approximately ℓ+ α + S(t).
   The veriﬁcation attributed to stored responses requires care. A stored answer was veriﬁed
for the situation in which it was produced. Reuse is warranted only when the present instance
preserves the conditions on which that veriﬁcation depended, and a similar but different in-
stance may fail them, which is what the assessment cost α pays for and what the fallback
covers. Habitual responses can also be acquired without any veriﬁed deliberate solution, by
imitation or by reinforcement of outcomes, and nothing here denies that. The claim is con-
ditional. Where a stored response derives from an evaluated solution and the conditions of
that evaluation are preserved, its present speed is no evidence that evaluation never occurred,
and the idea that a habitual response was never checked cannot be inferred from its speed.


5  The Routing Argument

A two-systems theory needs an assignment of tasks to systems. Let ρ  : T →{1, 2} be the
assignment and let r(t) be the cost of computing it. Suppose the routed agent pays r(t) and


                                        6

then pays Cρ(t)(t) under the selected system, so that its total cost is

                                    Crouted(t) = r(t) + Cρ(t)(t).                                   (3)


Proposition 4 (Routing must be cheaper than the saving).  If the speed advantage of System 1 on
a task t is to survive routing, then r(t) < C2(t) −C1(t).

Proof. The routed cost on a System 1 task is r(t) + C1(t), which beats the System 2 cost C2(t)
only if r(t) < C2(t) −C1(t).

   The proposition permits cheap routing between distinct mechanisms, and it does not show
that every cheap router is a memory lookup. The argument for parsimony is narrower. In
the model of Equation (2), the operations that determine whether a stored response is used
are retrieval and applicability assessment, whose cost ℓ+ α is paid on every encounter and
which already settle whether the fast route succeeds. A routing policy could use a cheap
cue, a task identiﬁer, or a learned estimate of retrieval success without performing retrieval
itself, so a separate dispatcher is not impossible. The model shows only that a dispatcher is
unnecessary for its speciﬁed execution policy, in which the success of the fast route is settled
by steps already paid for. A router added to it would need to be justiﬁed by evidence that
its cue carries information the retrieval steps do not, and the speed evidence discussed here
does not supply that. A serious alternative is the expected value of control account (Shenhav,
Botvinick and Cohen 2013), in which control is allocated by weighing the expected beneﬁt
of a control signal against its effort cost, and the signals selected vary in intensity as well
as in identity. This is a speciﬁed mechanism of control allocation and not an unexplained
supervisor, so it is not open to the objection below, and it ﬁts the position taken here to the
extent that the allocation it describes is graded. It also shows the shape that a defensible two-
mechanism account would take, namely a stated cost-beneﬁt policy whose inputs and outputs
can be tested, with the retrieval and assessment policy of Equation (2) as one competitor, in
place of a categorical sorter justiﬁed by the speed of the outcome. This is also where the
supernatural reading can enter, though only under one condition. Two mechanisms need not
be coordinated by an agent-like supervisor, and a learned mechanical routing policy raises
no difﬁculty of this kind. The objection applies when the sorter is taken to be a supervisor
that surveys each thought, judges it easy or hard, and dispatches it, while its own intelligence
is left unexplained, because the supervisor is then the ﬁgure the dichotomy was meant to
explain. A retrieval and assessment step against a store of prior solutions requires no such
supervisor, and it is itself a candidate routing policy, of the graded kind discussed above.





                                         7

6 Why the Partition Looks Real


Three features of the evidence make a continuum look like two groups, and they induce three
different kinds of error: the ﬁrst is an error of selection, the second of salience, and the third
of inference.
   The ﬁrst is the selection of examples. Studies of fast intuitive judgement use tasks that are
easy for a typical adult, meaning tasks for which nh(t) is large in the sampled population, and
studies of deliberate reasoning use tasks for which it is small. If the label “System 1” is then
applied to the tasks with large n, the label predicts low cost by construction, and the ﬁnding
that System 1 tasks are cheap is a restatement of how the tasks were chosen.
   The second is the observer’s attention to the ends of the practice curve. A person remem-
bers the ﬁrst, halting attempt at a new appliance and the thousandth effortless one, and no
episode in between is marked. Naming the two ends gives the impression of two machines,
whereas the intermediate points exist and are unremarkable.
   The third is that the shape of a cost distribution underdetermines the architecture that
produced it. Suppose practice counts, treated as a continuous approximation to what are in
fact discrete counts, are distributed with density fN and cost is Y = c(N) with c as in Equation
(1). Since c is strictly decreasing and differentiable, the density of Y at c(n) is

                               (    )    fN(n)    fN(n) nβ+1
                                 fY c(n) =    =                     .                               (4)
                                               |c′(n)|       bβ

The factor nβ+1 is nonconstant, so it moves the locations of the density maxima and can
change their number. A unimodal distribution of practice counts can therefore yield a bi-
modal distribution of costs, and a bimodal distribution of practice counts can yield a uni-
modal one. A mixture of two mechanisms can likewise appear unimodal. Neither the pres-
ence nor the absence of bimodality in cost, taken by itself, identiﬁes the number of mecha-
nisms, and it follows that a bimodal histogram of response times does not, by itself, identify
two systems. This conclusion serves the broader argument better than a claim that a single
process cannot produce bimodality, since it shows that distributional appearance underdeter-
mines architecture in both directions.


7 An Illustration from a Cached Decision Architecture


A concrete case in which the split between reusable and request-speciﬁc computation is ex-
plicit is a recent family of “typed decision” models, which choose among a set of options,
judge a condition, or assign a score, and have been described by their authors with the lan-
guage of System 1, a description this essay does not adopt (Li and Wang 2026). The architec-
ture is used here only as an instance of the amortization in Equation (2), and no claim is made


                                         8

about its performance or about the authors’ evaluations. In it, each of K options is encoded
independently of the request into a vector together with per-layer key and value projections,
and these entries are stored. A request is encoded fresh, and a small decision stage reﬁnes
the request state by attending over the stored entries. The reported property relevant here is
that substituting cached entries for recomputed ones leaves every output unchanged in exact
arithmetic, because an entry depends only on the option.
   Let copt be the cost of encoding and projecting one option, and Creq the cost of encoding
the request and running the decision stage over prepared entries. If a fraction ρ ∈[0, 1] of the
K options is already in the store,

                            C(ρ) = Creq + (1 −ρ) K copt.                                  (5)

At ρ = 0 every option is computed afresh, and at ρ = 1 only the request-speciﬁc work remains.
The two ends correspond to what would be called slow and fast operation, and they are
produced by the same weights, the same procedure and the same decisions, differing only in
how much of the work has been done in advance. The cost is linear in ρ, so there is no value
of ρ at which the model changes into another kind of model. Unlike the memory of Equation
(2), retrieval here is exact, since an option is either in the store or it is not, and the applicability
step is trivial because an entry depends only on the option. The decision stage is also run
on every request even at full reuse, which is the architectural counterpart of the observation
that a habitual response is still a computation on the present situation, with some of its inputs
precomputed.
   The illustration separates two things that the label runs together. The low latency at high
reuse comes from the cache, and it is a cost property. The accuracy of the model on its de-
cision tasks comes from training on a very large number of decisions of that type, which is
practice, and the architecture exposes the amortized part as an explicit memory. The sensible
name for such a model describes what it does, namely typed-output decision with cached
option representations. The name of a supposed cognitive system adds a commitment, that
the category exists independently of the training and the caching that made the tasks cheap,
which the construction does not support.


8  Practice That Teaches a Procedure


The cached architecture shows practice acting through stored components. A second case
shows practice acting differently, and it matters because it blocks the inference that all learned
speed is retrieval. Progress-aligned recurrence (Wang et al. 2026) takes a pretrained language
model, repeats a block of its layers a variable number of times, and trains it on sequential
state-tracking tasks, such as following a series of swaps among ﬁve boxes and answering



                                         9

which item ends in a queried box. Its central training choice is that iteration k is trained to
predict the state after the ﬁrst k operations, so that each iteration has a deﬁned job, and its
second is to rescale the recurrent state to a ﬁxed norm after every iteration, which controls the
magnitude of the state so that a drifting scale does not change what the repeated transforma-
tion computes. A learned halting signal lets the model decide when to answer, and a variant
trained on preﬁxes of problems obtains the intermediate targets from ﬁnal answers alone.
   The reported results are speciﬁc. Trained on at most 32 moves, a small model achieves
95.5% full-state accuracy at 512 moves, sixteen times the training length, against 55.7% for the
best prior recurrent method and 0.8% for an explicit chain of thought on the same backbone.
Removing the norm anchoring reduces the extrapolation factor from 16 to below 2.2, and
replacing the progress-aligned targets with ﬁnal-answer supervision reduces it to at most 8.
A model with four times the core depth, and a recurrent model with additional iterations but
without the alignment, each extrapolate less than twofold. These are the authors’ reports on
synthetic tasks and mostly on one small backbone, and the paper itself notes that results on
larger backbones vary far more across seeds, that accuracy does not rise monotonically with
model size, and that on graph reachability every recipe stays below 3.5-fold extrapolation,
which the authors attribute to the absence of a canonical intermediate state at each iteration,
an explanation this essay does not rely on.
   Four consequences bear on the argument. First, practice here does not act by retrieving
complete solved instances, which is a distinction of the kind that Anderson (1982) draws be-
tween storing and compiling. It supports reusable sequential computation that can be applied
more times than it was applied in training, so an account of practice limited to amortized an-
swers is too narrow and should be broadened to the acquisition of computational competence.
The result does not show that the latent state alone implements a sufﬁcient transition state,
since the full prompt remains available at every iteration. Second, the amount of computation
applied is graded, being the number of iterations, an integer-valued and variable depth, and
a longer problem simply receives more of it. Third, the availability of extra computation is not
what makes it useful. A model that can iterate without the learned organization gains little
from more iterations, so the depth of computation depends on training history and not on
the architecture’s capacity to loop. Fourth, the extended computation runs without any gen-
erated intermediate text, and the explicit chain of thought on the same backbone collapses
on longer problems, so externalization is neither what makes extended computation possible
nor what distinguishes it.
   The paper also bears on the claim that a correct answer, once reached, simply persists.
The paper’s own models, trained with the number of iterations matched to problem length,
answer correctly at the matching iteration and degrade rapidly if run beyond it, which is why
a halting rule is needed, and the learned stopping rule that works best, which requires six of
eight consecutive iterations to conﬁrm completion, reaches 92.9% at sixteen times the training


                                        10

length against 98.7% at eight times, with wide variation across seeds. Obtaining an adequate
answer and preserving it through further computation are therefore different achievements,
and a theory of cost that identiﬁes the ﬁrst with the second will misdescribe the second.


9  What Remains of the Distinction


The partition claim is not supported by the evidence usually offered for it, and the observa-
tions that motivated it remain. Some responses are produced more cheaply than others, some
are accompanied by report and some are not, and some can be interrupted and revised while
others run to completion. These are real differences, and they are best treated as distinguish-
able dimensions that fall into three families. The ﬁrst family concerns history. One param-
eter is the number of relevant prior episodes, nh(t). A second is the distance d(t, m) from
the present task to the nearest stored case, together with whether the stored result carries a
warrant that applies. A third is whether the practiced competence takes the form of stored in-
stances or of a reusable procedure (Logan 1988; Anderson 1982). The second family concerns
execution, and its parameter is the depth of computation actually executed on the present
task. The third family concerns access to what was computed, and it comprises three proper-
ties that are often run together, although they are conceptually distinguishable and need not
be coupled. Externalization is whether intermediate states are written into a context where
they can be reread. Decodability is whether intermediate states can be recovered from the
system by a readout of a stated class, which in the recurrent case holds because the training
objective makes it so. Reporting is whether the agent produces an account of its process, and
an account need not correspond to what was computed. The recurrent model above is deep,
decodable by its trained readout and unexternalized, and a person’s practiced arithmetic may
be shallow and readily reported after the fact. These dimensions permit combinations that a
single fast-slow axis obscures.
  On this view the central thesis is that cost, automaticity and reportability do not by them-
selves establish cognitive kinds, and that explaining their variation requires an account of
learning history, representation, execution and reuse. A practiced response can be a compiled
form of an earlier deliberate one, and the cached architecture and the amortization model
show how. Practice can also install a procedure that is then run for longer, and the recurrent
model shows that too. What has not been established here is the stronger claim that every
form of deliberation is retrieval with less work precomputed, and the essay does not rely on
it. The vocabulary of two systems should be retained, if at all, as shorthand for the ends of
the practice axis, with the understanding that it names a region of a continuum, implies no
mechanism of sorting, and cannot be read off from speed.
